about: The words of the chain old_gods (Data/encounters/chain_old_gods_793.json; Design/content/chains/old_gods.md): a vow made to the sea in a bad hour, and the price of keeping it and of breaking it. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the five news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: nobody is named in the words but saints, Pope Gregory, Boniface, Willibrord, Liudger and the Roman on the stone, Marcus Secundinius Silvanus, who is real. The Latin the priest reads is the stone's own (an altar from Domburg, CIL XIII 8793, from memory and livius.org (?)); the English beside it is ours. Nothing is quoted from a translation: what the bishop says of Pope Gregory follows the letter of 601 in Bede (Historia ecclesiastica I.30) in our own plain words, and what the farm wife says of the idol by the creek follows Alcuin's Life of Willibrord c. 14 in ours. Nobody but the priest says the goddess's name, and he has met it in no book. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: A bad hour
The wind has backed and the sea comes over the quarter faster than two men can bail. The steersman and the hand each say what a man does now, and they do not say the same thing.
The worst first. She will not take much more of this.
Now what can be done. Promise Saint Martin a candle as long as her keel, and say it aloud so the men hear it.
Saint Martin's house is a long way off, and no road to it from here. The sea is here. It is in the boat with us. Promise it a share of what it lets you keep. My people do, and I am still above it.
He means his devils.
I mean whoever is listening. Somebody is. Somebody always is. Only say something, and say it now. A man who bargains gets a better price than a man who begs.
Vow Saint Martin a candle the length of her keel
Vow the sea a share of what it lets you keep
Promise nobody anything, and bail

You shout it into the wind: a candle the length of her keel, to Saint Martin at Traiectum. The steersman crosses himself with his free hand. Toward morning the wind goes round, and she is still afloat.
You say it to the water: a share of whatever comes safe to land. The hand pours the last of the ale over the side and says nothing. Toward morning the wind goes round, and she is still afloat.

You promise nothing and bail until your arms give out. Toward morning the wind goes round, and she is still afloat. Neither man thanks you for it. Both of them look at the sky as if it had been owed something.
What the dune gave up
The gales have cut a slice from the dune west of the houses. A grey stone the height of a child stands half out of the sand, and a woman with sheep is looking at it as she would at a stranger's dog.
It comes out after a hard blow, and the sand has it back by midsummer. My mother saw it twice. Do not ask me who she is. Nobody here knows.
A woman sitting, with a basket of apples on her knee. A dog. Under her foot, the front of a ship. And letters, for those who have letters.
There are green coins in the sand by her, with heads on them. And three little silver ones, of the kind my grandfather was paid in. Somebody laid those there, and not so long ago.
There was another one, by the creek. The bishop broke it in my mother's mother's time. Its keeper hit him with a sword and was dead in three days. So we are Christians here.
You promised the sea a share. I have not forgotten it. Now the sea shows you where other men paid theirs. I only say what I see.
Look, a ship under her foot. Somebody thanked her for a cargo once. A good cargo, if it paid for a stone. He will not have been the only one who meant to.
Cut the letters on a tally stick, as they stand
Lay a penny in the sand with the others
Pick the silver out of the sand
You cut the letters into a hazel stick, stroke for stroke, without knowing one of them. The woman watches. She says the bishop's clerk does it faster and understands as little.
You press a penny into the sand beside the three. The woman says nothing. Later a boy brings a cheese down to the boat and will not say who sent it.
You sieve the sand through your fingers: three thin pennies, and a handful of black ones that scrape white. Twenty-four pence by weight. The woman calls her sheep and goes without a word.
Whose stone
A quiet watch. The steersman and the hand have been not speaking about the stone since Walichrum, and now they are speaking about it.
It is an idol. The priests have a list of such things, stones and springs and the rest, and what is to be done with them. You tell a priest. He breaks it.

No, no. It is a tally, that is all it is. A man promised something in bad weather and paid when he came home, and he had it cut in stone so nobody could say he had not. I thought Frisians liked a paid debt. I have always said so of you.

East of the Lauwers there is an old law for the man who takes from a god's house. They lead him down to the sand the tide covers. I do not say it is still done. I say nobody there picks up silver beside a stone.
And we have silver aboard that was picked up beside a stone.
Here is one for the watch. I have all of this one, for once. What is owed to nobody you can see, and still falls due?
The tithe.
A vow. But yours is a good answer. A good one, mind.
The steersman is right: a priest should hear of it
The hand is right: it is a paid debt, and not ours
Tell them both to mind the sheet
The steersman nods and says no more about it. The hand goes forward and coils a rope that was coiled already.
The hand says nothing for once, which is how you know he agrees. The steersman says he will pray for the boat, and it sounds like a warning.
They both look at the sheet, which is where it should be, and then at you. The hand laughs first. The question is still aboard in the morning.
For goods kept safe
A priest of Saint Martin's has heard that a Dorestad boat lay at Walichrum when the dune opened. He has a wax tablet with him, and he asks what you saw.
You cut them as they stood? Good. Most men bring me what they think a thing says.
Our clerk was on the island for the tithe lambs and copied it. I want a second pair of eyes that were there. Was there a dog?
DEAE NEHALENNIAE OB MERCES RECTE CONSERVATAS. To the goddess Nehalennia, for goods kept safe. Then a man's name: Marcus Secundinius Silvanus, a dealer in pots with Britain.
And four letters at the foot: V, S, L, M. He paid his vow, gladly, as was due. A merchant on your own road, thanking a devil with a basket of apples.
I have not met her name in any book we have. That troubles me less than the three silver pennies. Those are not Roman. Somebody's grandfather laid them there.
Your steersman says you owe the saint a candle the length of your keel. Saint Martin is patient. He is also exact.
And I am told you promised something to the sea. To the sea. As if it kept a tally.

The blessed Willibrord broke one on that island with his own hands. This one should not stand till midsummer for fools to lay pennies at. Be there in spring. I will send a clerk. See that it is ended decently.
Pay for the candle: wax the length of her keel
Take his errand to the island, and promise no more
Thank him for the reading; you carry goods, not mattocks

The wax is weighed and paid for, and the chandler measures your keel with a knotted cord and whistles. The candle will burn at the saint's altar from his feast until it is gone. The priest orders more wax of you, since you now know the price.
You say you will be at the island in spring and will see what is done. He writes something on his tablet. Then he asks whether you carry wax, and at what price.
He looks at you for a while, and then thanks you for coming. "I shall send a clerk with a mattock. You may at least not stand in his way."
Winter's start at Hleidr
A Danish skipper who knows your hand of old is loading for the islands. His lord keeps the feast at winter's start in the hall at Hleidr, and the hall is short of drink.
So this is the Frisian. Your hand tells me you made a promise in bad weather. Everybody has. Not everybody is asked about it afterward.
My lord kills a horse at winter's start and feeds the district. The meat is boiled, the ale goes round, a share is set aside. That is all it is. Strangers make more of it than we do.
Every ninth year it is a great one, they say, and a stranger does well to be elsewhere. This is not that year.
He wants wine on the table for the ones who count. Six casks from the Rhine, here on this jetty, before the first frost. I carry them over with mine. He pays like a lord, which is late and too much.
A share promised to the sea is paid where the sea is honoured. I know of no such place in your country. Not one. I know of one in his.
Go and see it once. I would, in your place. You sell to these people, and it helps to know what they do when they are not buying.
Take the order for the wine, and the seat that goes with it
Ask to come as a guest and carry nothing
Wish his lord a good feast and say you winter at home

He spits in his palm and you strike hands on six casks. "There is a seat for the man who brings the drink. Low down, but under the roof." He adds that wine at Hleidr is worth half as much again until the feast is over.
"Then come with empty hands and a good appetite. There is a seat, low down, but under the roof." He adds, for nothing, that wine at Hleidr is worth half as much again until the feast is over.
"A man should winter where his hearth is." He does not sound offended. "The seat is kept all the same. My lord keeps more seats than he fills."
A swell with no wind
The air is still and the sea is not. A long swell comes in from the north-west under a sky the colour of a knife, and both your men have stopped what they were doing to look at you.
No wind, and a swell like that. I have seen it twice. Both times there was a man aboard who owed something.
The candle is not burned. I am the steersman. I say what I see.
You said a share. A share, that was the word. I heard you. So did it.
I do not say it is angry. The sea counts slowly, that is all. It does count.
This is not the first time I have had to say it.
Put a purse over the side, now, whoever is owed
Say the vow again, aloud, with a day on it
A swell is a swell. Shorten sail and stand on
Forty pence in a knotted cloth goes over the side and is gone without a splash you can hear. The hand breathes out. By evening the swell has flattened, and there is a small honest wind.
You say it again, aloud, and put a day on it: before four moons are out. The men go back to their work. The swell runs on under you till dark, and then it is only sea.
You shorten sail and stand on. The gale passes north of you in the night with a noise like carts on a bridge. In the morning the men are quiet and do not meet your eye.
The gale that was behind the swell finds you at dusk. It takes the water cask, a spar and most of a night. Thirty pence will make it good. Neither man says he told you so, and both of them could.
The grey from the lord's field
The hall at Hleidr is full to the doors and smells of boiled meat and wet wool. The lord's steward finds you a place on a bench near the bottom, and a bowl is coming down the table toward you.
You are the Frisian the skipper spoke for. Sit there. Nobody here will ask what you believe. They will see what you eat.
It is the grey from the lord's own field. He was a good horse. A share has gone where shares go, and the rest is for the district.
You have wine aboard, I hear. The lord says the Rhine's is thin. He has never yet sent a cask back.
Eat or do not eat. That is yours to say, not mine. But decide before the bowl reaches you. A man who looks into the bowl and thinks is remembered longer than either.
Your steersman has stayed with the boat. He says somebody should. He is right, mind. Somebody should.
Eat what the hall eats
Take bread and ale, and pass the bowl on with both hands
Thank him, and eat aboard with the steersman

It is dark meat, sweet, boiled soft. You eat it with your fingers like everybody else. The man beside you shifts along the bench to give you room, and that is all that happens. Somebody will tell it at home.
You take bread and a horn of ale and hand the bowl on with both hands. The bench laughs. An old woman across the table says the Christians fast so often it is a wonder they have the strength to row.
You eat cold bacon aboard with the steersman, who says the blessing twice. Light and noise come down from the hall half the night. In the morning a boy is sent to fetch you up to the yard.
Three slips of wood

In the morning an old man of the district sits in the yard with a white cloth on his knees and three slips of wood. He lifts one for anybody whose question can be answered yes or no. The hand has told him yours.
You promised a share in a storm, and you are not sure it was heard. That can be asked.
You promised your own god's man a candle, and you want to know whether the ones here mind. That can be asked.
You promised nobody anything and came through, and it sits badly. You want to know whether something is owed. That can be asked.
I lift one slip. It says yes or it says no. It does not say why, and neither do I.
If you are paying, the share goes into the water off the point, not into my hand. I am told the Christians do it the other way.
He is the one the lord asks before he sails. The lord himself. I have seen the lord stay home.
Give the share to the water off the point
Put the question, and watch him lift a slip
Tell him you came to sell, not to ask
Forty pence of cut silver, weighed and knotted in cloth. You wade out off the point to the knee and let it go. The old man nods once. The hand says, in your own tongue, that it is done and well done.
He moves the slips about under the cloth and lifts one. "Yes." He puts it back with the others. That is all of it. The men are easier on the way down to the boat.
He moves the slips about under the cloth and lifts one. "No." He puts it back with the others. He will not lift a second, and he will not say what you should do about it.
"Then sell." He is not put out. "The lord's hunters are down from the woods with marten and want it gone before the snow. They will take a low price this month." It is true.
A priest hears things
The priest of Saint Martin's has a small book open on his knee and a finger in it. He has had word of you from the island, or from the north, or from your own steersman's face.
You ate horse at a heathen table. The blessed Boniface had it from the pope himself that this is unclean. Men come home from the north and think nobody saw.
You gave silver to the sea for a promise. Silver that might have fed the poor of Dorestad, of whom there is a multitude.
You laid a penny at that stone. So there are four silver ones now.
You took silver from the sand beside it. I do not grieve for a devil's purse. But the islanders say you robbed her, and they say it as Christians should not.
The book gives a term for each thing. I have added it up. Forty days on bread, salt and water, and no meat before Easter.
Or the term may be turned into alms. It is done everywhere. I do not like it, and I take it. Forty-eight pence, to the poor, through my hand.
Take the forty days
Turn the term into alms
Say he has been told sailors' stories
Forty days of bread and salt. You trade thin and sleep badly, and the steersman keeps the fast beside you without being asked. At the end of it the priest gives you his hand.
Forty-eight pence on his table. He counts it, writes it down, and says the poor will pray for you by name. He does not say he thinks better of you.
"Sailors' stories," you say. He closes the book on his finger and looks at you a long time. "Then I was told wrong." He does not believe it, and he cannot show otherwise.
"Sailors' stories," you say. "Your steersman came to me on Sunday," he says, "for himself, and wept for you." He closes the book. He will know your sail when he sees it.
Before midsummer
The stone stands clear to its foot. The sheep woman is there with two neighbours, and a young clerk from Traiectum with a mattock and a mule. Everybody has been waiting for somebody else to begin.
By midsummer the sand takes her back. It always has. I would let it. But nobody asks me.
The priest's word is that it is to be broken, or else signed with the cross and made honest. Whatever lies under it is the church's and the king's. He said you would know which.
I am sent to see it and say what I saw. I was not sent to lift a mattock alone among these people.
My neighbours say stand her up and leave her be. Skippers ask after her already. One from over the sea left apples.
You have paid for that night. This is not your debt now. That is the best time to decide a thing. I forget who told me that. I believe it.
I was beside you that night. Whatever you do here, do it as a man who was in that storm.
Take a shovel and give her back to the sand
Set her upright on a footing of turf, facing the sea
Have the clerk cut a cross on her and bless the ground
Take the mattock

You take the shovel from a neighbour's hand and begin. After a while the women help, and then the clerk, who is young and has nothing else to do. By evening there is a hump of sand, and after the next blow not even that.
It takes six people and the mule to walk her upright onto a bed of cut turf. She faces north-west, where the weather comes from. The clerk will not touch the rope. He rides for Traiectum before dark.

The clerk cuts a cross above her head with a chisel, deep, and says the words over the ground with a bowl of salt and water. The islanders watch. One of the neighbours asks if it is a church now. He says it will be.
It takes eleven blows. The apples go first. Under the foot of the stone the sand is green, and then it rattles. The clerk goes down on his knees in it. The sheep woman has already gone.
Midsummer sand

The dune is whole again. Where the stone stood there is marram grass and a sheep track. The sheep woman has her neighbours with her, and something to say to the Dorestad man who used a shovel when he was handed a mattock.
The clerk went home with nothing to break. The Danes who call here saw nothing to ask about. We are left alone. That is all we wanted.
We have no silver to speak of. We have cloth. Fourteen bolts, from every house a share. Do not say no. They have already argued about who gave most.
And we know this water. The banks off the point have drowned better boats than yours. My brother will take you through on the ebb until you can take yourself.
If you want wool kept dry here and a true tally cut, there is a house. That we do not offer to everybody.
She will come out again after some hard blow. Not in my time, I hope. Let whoever finds her then have as much sense.
Take the cloth, and go out with her brother on the ebb
Take both, and ask for the house she spoke of
Say a shovel of sand is not a debt; take the pilot's teaching only
Fourteen bolts go aboard. For three ebbs her brother stands at your shoulder and names every bank and gut from the creek to the open sea, and makes you say them back.

Fourteen bolts go aboard, and over three ebbs her brother teaches you the banks. The house is the third from the creek, dry, with a loft. Her sister's husband will keep your wool there and cut a tally you can trust.

She looks at you as she looked at the stone. Then she sends her brother down to the boat anyway, and he teaches you the banks over three ebbs. The cloth stays. The island tells the story for years, and in it you are taller.
The stone under the altar

A chapel of turf and oak stands on the dune at Walichrum now, and the stone with a cross cut in it is the foot of its altar. At Traiectum the bishop has asked for the man who would not let it be broken and would not let it be bowed to.
The islanders already say the blessed Willibrord bled upon that stone. He did not. I have stopped correcting them.

Pope Gregory wrote to the English that a well-built shrine should be cleansed and kept, so that people come to the place they know and find God in it. You did as the pope advised, without having read him.
I wanted it broken. I was wrong, and I have said so, once.
He paid the saint his candle too, to the inch. I measured the keel myself.
Saint Martin has wine from his own slopes and a seal that toll men can read. You shall have some of each.
Take the wine, the silver and the seal
Take them, and ask for a chip of the stone for the house
Ask only that the boat be blessed

Eight casks from the church's cellar, twelve score pence, and a strip of parchment under Saint Martin's seal that says you carry for the church. The toll man at the bank looks at the seal twice and waves you through.

The bishop sends for the flake the chisel struck off when the cross was cut. It is the size of a thumbnail, sewn in linen. "It lay under a devil and now it lies under an altar. Keep it in the house, and tell the story straight." The wine, the silver and the seal come with it.

He comes down to the bank himself and signs the boat from stem to stern with a wet branch. Then he gives you the seal anyway. "A man who asks for nothing must be given something, or he becomes hard to bear."
Apples in the sand

She stands on a footing of turf with her back to the houses. There are apples at her foot, a cheese, a string of beads, and more silver pennies than there were. A Danish ship lies off the beach, and her skipper is wading ashore with something wrapped in cloth.
They come now. English, Franks, your Danes. Nobody says a name, because nobody has one. They put a thing down and go.
The clerk came back once and counted what lay there. Then he went away again. I think he was told to count.
The lord at Hleidr has heard there is a place on the Frisian side where a seaman can pay what he promised. He finds that a civil thing in a Christian country. He asked who was behind it.
He sends a ring from his own arm, to be kept whole. And four hundred pence by weight, and marten, because a lord's thanks should be heavy.
And he says this. Lay your goods with his, and two keels go where one went. We have a word for it. You will learn the word.
The priest at Traiectum knows your name. I would not sell wax there this year.
Lay your goods with his lord's: two keels where one went
Take the ring and the partnership, as a man whose word was good
Take the ring and the lord's thanks, and keep your own keel

You strike hands over the silver, and witnesses are called up from the beach. The ring goes back to Hleidr with your thanks: a man does not take a lord's ring and his goods both, unless his word is known. The second keel sails in spring.

The skipper has asked about you along the coast. What he heard was that you paid what you promised, to the one you promised it to. "Then both," he says. The ring goes on your arm, and witnesses are called up from the beach.
You take the ring, the silver and the furs, and say your own keel is enough for one house. He is not offended. "Then show the ring at any jetty of ours. They will know whose friend you are."
Two parts to the king

Under the stone lay a pit of coin: green bronze by the basket, blackened silver, and three thin pieces of gold. It has been weighed at Traiectum before the count's man, and the weights checked twice by people who do not trust each other.
Two parts to the king, as when Liudger broke the shrines in the east. One part to Saint Martin. The finder is paid out of Saint Martin's part, not the king's. I say so in case there is doubt.
The islanders will not sell you a fleece this year. They will come round. People do, when the thing is gone and the sky has not fallen.
The bishop puts his hand over you for this. In his courts, and against other lords' men, you are Saint Martin's.
I had the face of the stone brought here before the rest was burned for lime. I looked for her name once more in our books. It is not there. Now it is nowhere.
I will row for you. I will not leave you short of a man. I have rowed for worse. Do not ask me to sit near you in the next storm.
Take the finder's share and the bishop's hand
Give your share to the poor of Saint Martin's
Send half your share back to the island, for their broken dune

Two pounds and eight ounces are counted out to you by tale: six hundred and forty pence, some so old the heads are worn to thumbs. The count's man watches every one. The king's part goes up to Noviomagus under guard.

You push the silver back across the table. The priest is silent, then sends for the bishop. You leave with no pence, the bishop's hand over you, and Saint Martin's seal for the toll man. The poor of the church eat meat on a Sunday and are told whose it was.
You take half, and send half down the river with a man you trust, for the island, with no message. At the next shearing a boy brings a fleece to your boat at Walichrum and names a fair price.
This year the gales cut the dune at Walichrum, and a stone of the old people stood out of the sand: a woman seated, with a dog and a basket of apples. Nobody there could say who she was.
At Walichrum the sand has covered the stone again before midsummer. The bishop's clerk came home with a clean mattock.
This year a chapel was raised on the dune at Walichrum, over a stone of the old people that the bishop's clerk signed with the cross. The islanders say the blessed Willibrord bled on it.
On the dune at Walichrum a stone of the old people stands upright, and seamen of every people lay apples and pennies at it. The priests at Traiectum are not pleased, and the stone is still there.
This year a stone of the old people was broken on the dune at Walichrum, and a pit of old coin found under it. Two parts went to the king and one to Saint Martin.

A small open boat in a gale at dusk, the sail down to a rag, green water coming over the quarter. A broad Frisian at the steering oar with a wooden cross at his throat is shouting; a broad dark-bearded Northman bails with a bucket and looks at the sea, not at him.

A fresh-cut dune face on a grey morning after a gale. A weathered limestone altar stands half out of the sand: a seated woman, a basket of apples, a dog, a ship's prow under her foot, worn letters below. A woman in a dark hood with sheep behind her looks at it; small coins lie in the sand.

The boat under easy sail on a calm evening, low sun. The steersman at the oar and the hand on a thwart are turned toward each other, the one pointing aft toward land already out of sight, the other holding up a notched tally stick.

The porch of a timber church at Traiectum in thin autumn light. A tonsured priest in a dark tunic holds a notched hazel stick close to his eyes in one hand and a wax tablet in the other; the merchant waits, cap in hand; the river and a moored boat behind.

A plank jetty on the river at Ripa under a wide pale sky. A heavy Danish skipper in a blue cloak sits on a cask with his hand out to strike a bargain; the grey-haired hand stands beside him with folded arms; beads and combs on a stall behind, a ship loading.

A windless afternoon at sea under a hard steel-grey sky. The sail hangs slack while a long oily swell lifts the boat. The steersman and the hand have both stopped work and are looking straight at the viewer.

Inside a great timber hall at night, seen from a low bench by the door: a long fire, smoke under the roof, crowded tables, a wooden bowl of dark boiled meat being handed down the table toward the viewer. A steward with a staff stands near; far off at the high seat a lord drinks from a glass cup.

A fenced yard beside the hall on a cold bright morning, frost on the grass. An old man in a grey cloak sits on a stool with a white cloth over his knees and three small slips of wood on it, one lifted between finger and thumb. The fjord lies behind, with a low point running out into it.

A bare room by the church at Traiectum, lit by one small window. The priest sits with a small book open on his knee and one finger in it, looking up without expression. The merchant stands. A balance and a few pennies lie on the table between them.

The dune in early summer, larks up, the sea pale behind. The stone stands clear to its foot in a scoop of sand. Around it, apart from one another: the sheep woman and two neighbours with a wooden shovel, a young tonsured clerk holding a mattock beside a mule, and the grey-haired hand with his thumbs in his belt.

The same dune at midsummer, whole again, marram grass and a sheep track where the stone stood. In front, bolts of grey-blue cloth stacked on the sand by the beached boat; the sheep woman with her arms folded; behind her a man points out over the banks, where the ebb shows brown water.

A hall of the bishop's house at Traiectum. An old bishop in a white alb and dark cloak, with a plain curled staff, holds out a strip of parchment with a wax seal hanging from it; the priest stands a step behind; wine casks are being rolled past the open door toward the river.

The stone upright on a bed of turf at the top of the beach, facing a bright windy sea. Apples, a cheese, a string of beads and small coins lie at its foot. A Danish ship lies off; her skipper wades ashore holding up a silver arm-ring; the sheep woman watches from the side.

A table in a storeroom at Traiectum by lamp and daylight. Heaps of green bronze coin, a smaller heap of black silver, three gold pieces set apart; a balance; the count's man in a good cloak with his hand flat on the largest heap; the priest holding a broken piece of carved stone with part of a basket of apples on it.
